analysis.one_liner: Gives federal employees a 4.3% pay raise — a 3.3% across-the-board increase plus 1% more in locality pay — for 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill to give federal workers a 4.3% pay raise in 2026 sits in the House Oversight Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would raise pay for civilian federal employees in 2026: a 3.3% across-the-board increase for workers under the government's standard pay systems and for hourly wage-scale employees, plus an extra 1% increase in locality pay, which adjusts salaries for regional cost of living. In total, a 4.3% raise for roughly two million federal workers. The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and has received no action since; it has not been debated or voted on. The regular annual pay-adjustment process, not this bill, will set 2026 raises unless Congress moves it.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal employees would gain directly: salaried civil servants, hourly prevailing-rate workers such as mechanics and maintenance staff, and employees in expensive regions who benefit from the extra locality pay. Their households and the local economies around federal installations benefit indirectly.

how_it_helps.text: Raises basic pay under the statutory pay systems by 3.3% for calendar year 2026, lifting take-home pay for salaried federal workers from agency staff to senior career officials.
Raises pay for prevailing rate employees — hourly wage-scale workers such as mechanics, maintenance workers, and other blue-collar federal jobs — by 3.3% for fiscal year 2026.
Adds a 1% across-the-board locality pay increase, which matters most for employees in high-cost areas where federal salaries lag private-sector equivalents.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally, through higher federal payroll spending. There is no offset in the bill; the roughly $25-30 billion annual cost of a raise of this size (per general estimates of federal pay adjustment costs) would add to the deficit or displace other spending.

drawbacks.text: The raise applies to all roughly 2 million federal employees regardless of performance, adding a fixed payroll cost for taxpayers with no corresponding change in workload, staffing, or output.

By dictating both base pay (3.3%) and locality pay (1%) in statute, the bill bypasses the normal annual process in which the President proposes an adjustment based on private-sector wage data and fiscal conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For federal workers and the communities where they live, a 4.3% raise against inflation is a meaningful benefit. The cost is spread across all taxpayers as part of federal compensation spending, which is substantial in aggregate but modest per taxpayer. An honest caveat: a legislated raise forecloses the President's ability to adjust the number to fiscal conditions, and federal pay already includes benefits many private-sector workers lack. On balance the bill is a straightforward transfer to a large, politically organized workforce, at general taxpayer expense.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which never acted on it, so it never reached the House floor for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Connolly introduced the bill on January 16, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

No hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the only subsequent entry in the action history is September 16, 2025, when Representative Walkinshaw was allowed to assume first sponsorship — a step taken after Representative Connolly's death so the bill could keep adding cosponsors.
With the bill still in committee and the 119th Congress running through January 2027, it remains technically alive but has shown no movement toward a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal employees are worse off, since the raise they were promised has not materialized and the standard annual adjustment will set their pay instead. Taxpayers benefit marginally from the saved cost. No private industry is affected either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, marginally; federal workers lost a raise

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is almost entirely Democratic — 35 of 36 cosponsors are Democrats with a single Republican — though no vote has occurred to test the split.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is a 4.3% combined raise for federal workers. It stalled, so they gain nothing.
The raise would be paid from the federal budget, which all taxpayers fund. Because the bill died, taxpayers avoid that added cost.

analysis.trajectory: As a pay-raise bill with nearly all-Democratic sponsorship sitting in a committee controlled by Republicans, it is unlikely to get a hearing or markup. Federal raises are more typically set through the annual appropriations process or the President's pay letter, so this bill will most likely die quietly at the end of the Congress.
